arc_intro:
FQ-156 — Priya Nair (Cloud Architect)

Time to actually close this out. We know a peering connection used to exist where that 10.50.0.0/16 route points, and we know notification-worker is still weekly trying to reach a specific address inside it. Before we touch anything on the AWS side, I want you to go straight to the source — check notification-worker's own scheduled jobs directly. Whatever's making that weekly call is going to explain the rest of this.

While you're at it — we're also finally ready to set up real peering, for real reasons this time. ananya-analyst's analytics VPC needs a private connection to pull order data without going over the public internet. Let's do that one properly, so you see what 'done right' actually looks like next to what we're about to find.

— Priya
arc_outro:
Priya Nair — FQ-156 update:

And there it is. Eight months of a dead cron job, a route nobody removed, and a TODO comment that just... sat there. Not a breach, not anything sinister — just exactly the pattern this whole ticket has been about since C3.1. Someone did the responsible thing when QuickCourier ended (deleted the peering connection), and then the less-visible cleanup — the route, the script, the scheduled job — just never got finished. That's the real story of this entire VPC, not just this one route.

Good work getting the analytics peering done properly on the first try, too — you clearly understood what 'update both route tables' actually means, not just the concept.

Next: Route 53. We've built the network. Now let's make sure people can actually find it by name, not just by IP.

— Priya

tasks.diagnosis: Eight months ago, FoodQuick ran a short pilot integration with a hyperlocal delivery partner called QuickCourier, connected via a direct VPC peering connection (pcx-0e4a9f2b1c8d3a1f2) to QuickCourier's own VPC (10.50.0.0/16), so notification-worker could privately check courier status at 10.50.13.4 without going over the public internet. The pilot ended and QuickCourier's AWS account was decommissioned — someone correctly deleted the peering connection at that point. But three related cleanup items were left behind: the now-dangling static route in rtb-main (found in C3.1), the weekly cron job on notification-worker that keeps trying the now-nonexistent endpoint (found here), and a TODO comment in the script itself that explicitly says to remove it — written 8 months ago, never acted on.
tasks.fix: This is not a security incident — the peering connection was correctly deleted when the partnership ended. The remaining cleanup is: (1) disable and remove the cron job on notification-worker, (2) remove the now-fully-understood dangling static route from rtb-main, (3) delete or archive the check_courier_status.sh script, (4) document in the decommissioning runbook that partner integrations need route table AND scheduled-job cleanup, not just the peering connection itself.
tasks.explanation: This whole CS3 session's real theme — 'set up once in a rush, never fully cleaned up.' This a breach not, a attack not — a TODO comment 8 months ignore do, that real story. in Engineering this very common — one person nalla intention's delete do (peering connection), but related cleanup items across different systems (route table, cron job, script file) easily miss will happen.

tasks.scenario: Ravi asks for the numbers before approving the Transit Gateway migration: VPC Peering itself has no hourly charge (only data transfer costs apply, same as peering). Transit Gateway costs roughly ₹2.90/hour per attachment (~₹2,100/month per VPC attached) PLUS a small per-GB data processing charge, similar in structure to NAT Gateway's pricing.
tasks.question: For FoodQuick's near-term plan (3 VPCs now, expecting 5-6 within a year), how should the cost trade-off be framed?
tasks.solution: At 3 VPCs, Transit Gateway costs roughly 3 × ₹2,100 ≈ ₹6,300/month in attachment fees alone, versus effectively free peering connections (data transfer costs are comparable either way) — peering looks cheaper today. But full-mesh peering at 6 VPCs would need 15 separate connections to manage, each with its own route table entries on both sides, versus Transit Gateway staying at a flat per-VPC attachment cost with ONE central route table to manage. The ₹6,300/month is best framed as paying for reduced operational complexity and fewer chances of a repeat of the exact kind of partial-cleanup mistake just found with QuickCourier — not as a raw peering-vs-TGW price comparison.
tasks.explanation: This cost analysis's real point — cheapest option ippo only looking at not, GROWTH trajectory's operational complexity cost-ai think. TGW's real value — fewer moving parts, fewer places anything miss aaga chance.
